# goal.js

> goal.js is a compiled JavaScript framework where `var` is state and `let`/`const` are computed. Pages are rendered on the server and resumed in the browser, with no hydration: each component's code loads on its first event, in a small chunk of its own, and a page with no events ships no JavaScript. It is secure by default. The npm package is `goaljs`.

What to know before writing goal.js code:

- Source files are `.goal`: JavaScript with JSX, plus `route METHOD /path/{param} { ... }` blocks at the top level, `{if (a) X else if (b) Y else Z}` in markup, `server function` declarations, an optional `#strict` first line that turns on type checking, and an optional `style { ... }` block of CSS scoped to the file.
- A component is a top-level function with a capitalised name that ends in `return <element>`: one element, one `return`. It takes one parameter, its props.
- `var` at the top of a component declares state, one name per `var`. `let` and `const` are computed: worked out again from the state on each run. State changes only in event handlers, by assignment (`count++`, `items = [...items, x]`), never while rendering, and arrays and objects are replaced, not changed in place.
- These are compile errors: `var` anywhere else in a component; assigning a `const`, an import or a route's path parameter; a handler assigning a prop or a computed value; a component assigning a variable declared at the top of the file.
- Markup uses HTML names: `onclick`, `oninput`, `onsubmit`, `class`, `for`, `value`, `checked`. There is no `className`, `onClick`, `bind:`, `@`, `:` or `$`. An event handler is a function; a string of code is a compile error. A form with `onsubmit` never reloads the page.
- Components have no `async`, `await` or `fetch`. To reach the server, export a `server function` and call it from an event handler like a plain function; goal.js sends the request and the page updates when it answers.
- To load data as a component renders, write `var found = call(search(q))` at the top of the component, with a server function call inside. `found` is state: `value` (undefined until the first answer), `loading`, `error`, `reload()` and `cancel()`. The server renders the page with the answer; in the browser the call runs again when its arguments change, and a newer request stops the one before it.
- A route's body runs on the server once per request and may use `await`. Path parameters are plain constants (`id`). `request` has `method`, `path`, `url`, `params`, `query`, `headers`, `cookies`, `form`, `files`, `json` and `signal` (aborted when the client goes away). A route returns markup (a page), `redirect('/path')`, `json(value, status, headers)`, `reply(body, { status, type, headers })` (markup, text or bytes), `stream(asyncIterable, options)`, `events(asyncIterable)` (server-sent events, each value as JSON), `notFound()`, or nothing (204), and `cookie(name, value, options)` sets a cookie.
- `group /admin { before { ... } route GET / { ... } }` puts routes under one path; `before` runs first (outer groups' first), and one that returns something answers instead of the route. `group /api api { ... }` makes API routes: no CSRF check, no cookies read or set, any body in `request.body` (a Buffer), errors as JSON, and other sites may read answers only when goal.config.js `cors` allows (a list of origins, or '*'); preflights are answered.
- Lists are `items.map((x) => <li key={x.id}>...</li>)`. With `key`, the list is patched by key.
- Components can render components, pass `children`, and pass function props that run as the parent's handlers.
- One compile makes a file's server code and browser code, from the same templates and with the same escaping and URL checks, so the browser's renders always agree with the server's HTML. Routes and server functions never reach the browser.
- Security is on by default: every value is escaped, `<script>`, `<style>` and `srcdoc` in markup are compile errors, `javascript:` and `data:` URLs are blocked, every page has a strict Content-Security-Policy with a nonce, and forms and server functions are protected from CSRF. `goal.config.js` turns each one off explicitly.
- The CLI is `goal dev`, `goal build`, `goal start`, `goal check` and `goal add <tool>`. Static files go in `public/`, and `.env` is read into `process.env`.

## Docs

- [Getting started](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/getting-started): install goal.js, the CLI, a first app, and what goes in an app's folder
- [Routes](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/routes): `route METHOD /path/{param}`, the request, what a route returns, cookies, forms and file uploads
- [Components](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/components): state and computed values, markup, `{if}`, lists and keyed lists, components inside components, children, function props, scoped styles, compile errors
- [Server functions](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/server-functions): calling the server from a component, without `async` or `fetch`, and loading data with `call()`
- [Types](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/types): `#strict` files, checked before the app runs, and runtime checks of what reaches the server
- [Security](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/security): the defaults, how to change each one in `goal.config.js`, and reporting errors
- [How it works](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/how-it-works): parse, compile, render and resume; chunk sizes; live updates in `goal dev`; debugging
- [Vite](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/vite): working on an app inside Vite's dev server, and testing with Vitest
- [Tools](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/tools): `goal add` for Tailwind CSS, PostCSS, Prisma, Drizzle, ESLint, Prettier, Vitest, Playwright and Sentry

## Optional

- [Performance](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/performance): js-framework-benchmark results, a 100,000-row virtual list, and how to measure
- [All the docs in one file](https://goallabs.github.io/goal/llms-full.txt): every page above, as Markdown
- [Source code](https://github.com/goallabs/goal): the compiler, runtime, CLI and VS Code extension
- [Recipes for goal add](https://github.com/goallabs/goal/tree/main/recipes): how each tool is set up, and how to send a recipe
